label: The Gauss-Bonnet Theorem
notes: This chapter, printed pages 263 to 282, ties local curvature to global topology. We open with the promise of the climax: the integral of Gaussian curvature over a closed surface equals two pi times its Euler characteristic, a quantity fixed by topology alone and blind to the metric we chose.

label: Geodesic Curvature
notes: Before any integral theorem we need the right notion of bending. Geodesic curvature measures how far a curve on a surface deviates from being a geodesic, recording only the tangential turning seen from within the surface and discarding the normal bending forced by the ambient embedding.

label: Turning Angle and Exterior Angles
notes: Along a smooth boundary the unit tangent rotates continuously, and that rotation rate integrates the geodesic curvature. At a corner the tangent jumps; the exterior angle records that instantaneous turn. Together continuous turning and corner jumps account for the total rotation of the tangent.

label: The Gauss-Bonnet Formula for a Region
notes: The local Gauss-Bonnet formula balances three contributions over a polygonal region: the curvature integrated over the interior, the geodesic curvature integrated along the smooth edges, and the exterior angles summed at the vertices. Their total is exactly two pi, independent of the region's shape.

label: Geodesic Polygons
notes: When every edge is a geodesic the boundary integral vanishes, leaving curvature plus exterior angles equal to two pi. Rewriting exterior angles as pi minus interior angles converts the statement into a clean relation between total curvature and the sum of interior angles of the polygon.

label: Geodesic Triangles and Angle Excess
notes: For a geodesic triangle the formula says the sum of interior angles minus pi equals the integrated curvature over the triangle. This angle excess is positive where curvature is positive, zero in the flat plane, and negative on saddle-like surfaces, making curvature directly measurable by angles.

label: Spherical Triangle Example
notes: On a sphere of radius R the Gaussian curvature is the constant one over R squared, so the excess equals the area divided by R squared. A triangle with three right angles, an octant of the sphere, has angle sum three halves pi and area exactly one eighth of the total sphere.

label: From Local to Global
notes: To globalize we triangulate a compact surface and sum the local formula over every triangle. Interior edge integrals cancel in pairs because adjacent triangles traverse shared edges in opposite directions, and the vertex angles regroup into the combinatorial Euler characteristic of the triangulation.

label: The Euler Characteristic
notes: The Euler characteristic equals vertices minus edges plus faces and is a topological invariant independent of the chosen triangulation. For an orientable closed surface of genus g it equals two minus two g, so the sphere gives two, the torus gives zero, and higher genus gives negative values.

label: The Global Gauss-Bonnet Theorem
notes: The global theorem states that the integral of Gaussian curvature over a compact surface without boundary equals two pi times its Euler characteristic. The left side depends on the metric; the right side depends only on topology. Hence total curvature is a topological invariant, deformable but conserved.

label: Sphere versus Torus
notes: The sphere has Euler characteristic two, forcing total curvature four pi, so a metric of all-negative curvature is impossible there. The torus has characteristic zero, forcing total curvature zero, which is why the flat torus exists. Topology dictates what curvatures a surface may carry.

label: Consequences and Recap
notes: Gauss-Bonnet constrains geometry by topology: positively curved closed surfaces must be spheres or projective planes, and a flat metric forces Euler characteristic zero. We recap geodesic curvature, the local formula, angle excess, and the global identity linking total curvature to two pi chi.
